column2: Why need plasma concentration, receptor occupancy, and measured effect not change in parallel?
column3: Each link from free concentration at the site of action, through target engagement and signal transduction, to cellular, organ, and whole-person responses can amplify, buffer, delay, or oppose the one before it.

column2: Why does doubling ligand concentration usually fail to double receptor occupancy?
column3: Fractional occupancy equals concentration divided by concentration plus KD, a rectangular hyperbola that approaches full occupancy asymptotically, so it is near-proportional only at very low concentrations.

column2: How can two ligands with the same KD differ in how long they engage their target?
column3: Equilibrium affinity hides association and dissociation rates; residence time is roughly the reciprocal of the dissociation rate, so a slowly dissociating ligand can sustain engagement after free concentration falls.

column2: What distinguishes affinity from efficacy, and why can a partial agonist not reach the maximal response even at high occupancy?
column3: Affinity describes binding, whereas efficacy is the capacity of a bound ligand to generate a response; a partial agonist contributes less activation per occupied receptor, so it cannot reach the system's maximum.

column3: It occupies receptors while contributing less activation than the full agonist would, so the same molecule can appear agonistic or antagonistic depending on context.

column2: What distinguishes an inverse agonist from a neutral antagonist, and when does the difference become observable?
column3: An inverse agonist stabilises inactive conformations and reduces constitutive activity, while a neutral antagonist blocks agonist binding without changing basal activity; they differ visibly only when constitutive signalling is appreciable.

column3: While reserve is consumed the curve shifts rightward with unchanged Emax; once it is exhausted the maximum falls. Reserve varies among tissues, so one agonist can be full in one organ and partial in another.
